item.passage:
Coach Lund posted the order for the medley relay on the Thursday before the conference meet, and Theo read it standing in a puddle on the pool deck. Backstroke, Ana. Breaststroke, Joel. Butterfly, Theo. Freestyle, Priya Raman. Theo read it twice and decided the coach had made a mistake. Priya had been on the team for eleven days. Marcus, who had swum the last leg for two seasons, was listed at the bottom as an alternate.

In practice the trouble showed up at once. Theo would come into the wall at the end of his butterfly, and Priya would still be crouched on the block, watching. She waited until his hands struck the tile, and only then swung her arms and dove. Each exchange cost the team most of a second. Coach Lund timed six of them and said only, "Again."

After the sixth, Theo hung on the lane rope, breathing hard. "You can start moving before I touch," he said. "Your feet just have to stay on the block until I hit the wall."

"I know the rule," Priya said. She looked down the lane instead of at him. "At my old school I left early in the last relay of the season. The officials took our whole team out of the results. Four of us swam, and three of them had done everything right."

Theo thought about that on the bus home. He had been treating the slow exchanges as her problem, a habit she would have to fix on her own. But she could leave early only if she could count on his hands arriving when she expected them, and that part was his job, not hers.

On Saturday morning he found her by the warm-up lane. "Watch my arms," he said. "When they come over for the last stroke, start your swing. I'll be there. If I have to stretch that last stroke, I'll stretch it, but I'll be there."

The relay was the final event of the meet. Ana touched third. Joel pulled them up to second. Theo swam his fifty meters counting strokes, and on the last one he reached as far as his shoulders would let him. He felt the wall under his fingers and, in the same instant, saw her feet leave the block above him.

They finished second, three tenths of a second behind Westbrook. Beside each swimmer's name the scoreboard listed a number Theo had always ignored: the gap between one swimmer's touch and the next swimmer's takeoff. Beside Priya's it read 0.11. Marcus leaned over the railing, read it out loud, and slapped the water next to Theo hard enough to splash him.

The phone rang once at six, a recorded voice
reading the names of schools in a row,
ours somewhere in the middle, and my mother
said, Go back to sleep, which none of us did.

By eight the street had lost its edges.
The curb, the Dunns' low hedge, the line
where our yard ended and the road began
were under one white sheet, the same depth everywhere,

so that for a day it was only ground,
and anyone could walk on any of it.
Mr. Pruitt, who edges his lawn with scissors,
stood in the middle of the road in his boots

and lobbed a snowball at the Dunns' mailbox
and missed, and laughed, and tried again.
The hours lost their edges too. No bell
for math, and lunch was whenever

somebody thought of soup. We built a fort
against the buried hedge and argued all afternoon
about where the door should go, then knocked
a wall down by accident and called it the door.

At dusk the grown-ups came out with shovels
and dug the edges back, the curb first,
then the walk, then the strip along the hedge,
a little more of the line with every scrape,

and by morning the street was a street again,
the yard a yard, the hours numbered,
and the bus came down the cleared road at seven-ten
the way it always had.

I am the one with the shovel now.
I am out at six, digging the curb back
before anyone else is up, and some mornings
I lean on the handle a minute longer than I need to

and look at the street while it is still one piece,
the yard and the road and the hedge all the same white,
before I find the line again
and cut it clean.

Mrs. Brandt baked on Friday mornings, and by nine the smell came up the stairwell to our apartment on the third floor. The first time I knocked on her door, the fall I was twelve, I meant only to ask what it was. I left two hours later with flour to my elbows and a loaf wrapped in a dish towel.

Her bread began with a jar on the counter that she called the starter: flour and water she had kept going for nineteen years, fed every day with a little more of each. "It is alive," she said, tilting the jar so I could see the bubbles against the glass. Wild yeasts in the mixture fed on the flour and gave off gas, she explained, and that gas was what lifted a loaf. I thought she was exaggerating about the alive part until I watched the starter double in its jar over one afternoon.

That fall I baked with her most Fridays. She taught me to fold the dough instead of kneading it hard, to wet my hands so it would let go of them, and to wait. Waiting was most of it. A loaf took her the better part of two days, and for most of those hours the bread simply sat under a towel, doing something I could check only by pressing a finger into it and watching how slowly the dent filled.

In December she flew to visit her sister for three weeks and left the jar with me, with a note taped to the lid: Feed daily. Pour off half, then add flour and water. It will forgive a lot.

I tested that sooner than I meant to. I fed it carefully for a week, and then exams came, and I forgot it at the back of our counter for four days. When I opened the lid, a layer of gray liquid sat on top, and the smell made my eyes water. I was sure I had killed nineteen years of somebody else's bread.

My mother read the note on the lid again and told me to do what it said. So I poured off the liquid, threw out most of what was left, and fed the few spoonfuls at the bottom. The next morning there were a handful of bubbles. By the end of the week the starter was climbing the jar again, though it smelled sharper than before.

When Mrs. Brandt came home, I carried the jar downstairs and told her everything, the four days included. She lifted the lid, sniffed, and nodded. "Sharper," she said. "It had a hard week. It will settle." Then she spooned some of it into a second jar, screwed on the lid, and put it in my hands. "Now you have one of your own to forget," she said.

In 1879 Garrow's Landing was a town of about nine hundred people on the north shore of Lake Tamsin, and most of its families made their living from the water: fishing for whitefish, hauling lumber, or mending the nets and boats of those who did. Weather was everyone's business and no one's job. Old hands read the sky, the color of the water, and the behavior of the gulls, and they disagreed often enough that a captain could usually find support for whatever he had already decided to do.

Hester Quill taught the upper grades at the town school. That spring she bought a barometer from a catalog with her own money and hung it in the schoolroom, and three times a day, at seven, at two, and at nine, she wrote down its reading along with the temperature and the direction of the wind. Her pupils took turns reading the dial. Within a year she had noticed what weather observers elsewhere had long known: a steady fall in air pressure over several hours often came before a gale on the lake.

In 1881 she brought her notebooks to the town council and asked for two things: a flagpole on top of the grain elevator, the tallest structure on the shore, and twelve dollars for a set of flags. A red flag would mean a storm was likely within a day; a red flag above a white one would mean it was likely by nightfall. The council gave her the pole and six dollars. She sewed the rest of the flags herself.

The fishermen were slow to trust a schoolteacher's dial over their own eyes. That first summer several boats went out under the red flag, came home through choppy water, and reported that the weather had been nothing much. Then, on a clear morning in late September, the barometer fell faster than Quill had ever recorded. She raised both flags before eight. Nine boats stayed at the dock. Two went out anyway, and by afternoon the wind had swung around and built so quickly that both crews barely reached the breakwater, their sails torn.

After that the flags were watched. Captains learned to look up at the elevator before they looked at the sky, and children could tell visitors what each flag meant. Quill kept her readings for thirty-one years, long after she had stopped teaching, and when she died in 1912 her notebooks went to the county historical society, where they remain the longest daily weather record for that stretch of shore.

It is hard to name anyone in Garrow's Landing who did more with less: a borrowed idea, a catalog barometer, six dollars, and a needle. Weather was still everyone's business. It had become, at last, someone's job as well.

A young male zebra finch raised in a cage near its father will, by the time it is about three months old, sing a song very much like his. (In zebra finches, only the males sing.) Raise the same bird out of hearing of any adult of its kind, and it still sings, but the result is odd: a string of notes with an unusual structure, which female zebra finches appear to find less attractive. For this bird, much of its song is something it has to learn.

Not every bird works this way. A chicken or a dove raised alone produces calls much like those of its species, and so, as far as researchers can tell, do some flycatchers, such as the eastern phoebe. Learning a song from others seems to have arisen in only a few groups of birds: the songbirds, which make up roughly half of all bird species, along with the parrots and the hummingbirds.

In songbirds the learning happens in two stages, which can be separated in time. In the first, the young bird only listens. It hears adults sing and appears to store a memory of the sound, in some species for months, before it makes any attempt at a song of its own. White-crowned sparrows, studied closely since the 1960s, seem to do most of this memorizing in a window of a few weeks early in life; songs heard after that window have much less effect.

In the second stage the bird practices. Its first efforts, called subsong, are quiet and rambling, and they have often been compared to the babbling of a human infant. Over weeks the attempts grow louder and more structured, and pieces of the memorized model begin to appear. Eventually the song settles into a fixed form, and in many species it changes little for the rest of the bird's life.

To match its memory, the bird must hear itself. In experiments, birds deafened after the listening stage but before practice went on to produce songs at least as abnormal as those of birds raised without ever hearing an adult. The bird seems to compare what comes out of its own throat against the stored model and to adjust, attempt by attempt, until the two agree.

Because the learning is a kind of copying, small differences can be passed along. White-crowned sparrows in neighboring areas of the California coast sing recognizably different versions of their song, regional dialects that can last for decades. Researchers who study human speech have taken a strong interest in all of this: a period of early listening, a babbling stage, and a need to hear one's own voice are also features of how children learn to talk. How deep the resemblance goes is still debated, but few other animals offer so close a parallel.
